stops.title: The journey out of Africa
stops.blurb: Small groups had left Africa before, but their lines mostly died out. Then, between about 60,000 and 50,000 years ago, one population moved out through southwest Asia and kept going. Genetic studies show that everyone alive today whose ancestry lies outside Africa descends mainly from this one movement, by a group that probably numbered only in the thousands.

links.label: Recent African origin of modern humans

stops.dateNote: Genetic and fossil evidence put the main dispersal between about 60,000 and 50,000 years ago.

stops.title: Meeting the relatives
stops.blurb: The newcomers were not alone. Neanderthals had lived across Europe and western Asia for hundreds of thousands of years, and Denisovans further east. The groups met and had children together: people with ancestry outside Africa still carry about 2% Neanderthal DNA, from mixing dated to roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago. By about 40,000 years ago the Neanderthals were gone.
stops.dateNote: The mixing is dated from ancient genomes; the last Neanderthal sites date to about 40,000 years ago.

stops.title: Crossing the sea to Australia
stops.blurb: Even with seas far lower than today, no land bridge ever joined Asia to Australia and New Guinea, then a single continent called Sahul. People crossed from island to island over tens of kilometres of open water, which took boats or rafts and planning. Stone tools at Madjedbebe in northern Australia have been dated to 65,000 years ago; other researchers argue for about 50,000.
stops.debate: Clarkson and colleagues date the oldest tools at Madjedbebe to about 65,000 years ago. O'Connell and colleagues argue the tools may have moved down through the sand and that no site in Sahul is securely older than about 50,000 years.

stops.title: The oldest pictures and music
stops.blurb: On a cave ceiling in Sulawesi, Indonesia, someone painted three human-like figures around a wild pig. Mineral crusts that grew over the paint are at least 51,200 years old, which makes it the oldest known picture that tells a story. More than 35,000 years ago, people in what is now Germany were playing flutes carved from bird bone and mammoth ivory.
stops.dateNote: The date is a minimum age: the painting is older than the crust that covers it.

stops.title: The ice age at its peak
stops.blurb: Between about 26,500 and 19,000 years ago the ice sheets reached their greatest size. Ice covered Canada and northern Europe. So much water was locked up in it that the sea stood about 125 metres lower than today. Britain was joined to Europe, Siberia to Alaska, and New Guinea to Australia. People lived through it on every continent they had reached.

stops.title: Into the Americas
stops.blurb: The Americas were the last continents people reached. A camp at Monte Verde in Chile shows they were far to the south by about 14,500 years ago, probably after travelling down the Pacific coast. Fossil footprints at White Sands in New Mexico have been dated to between 23,000 and 21,000 years ago. If that holds, people arrived before the ice age peaked.
stops.debate: Whether people were in North America before about 16,000 years ago turns mostly on the White Sands footprints and how reliable their dates are.

p: People reached the Americas from northeast Asia. Their ancestors lived in and around Beringia, the land that joined Siberia to Alaska when the sea was low. From there they moved south past the North American ice sheets and spread quickly: by about 14,500 years ago there was a camp at Monte Verde in southern Chile, some 15,000 kilometres from Alaska.

Three kinds of evidence fit together. Genomes of living and ancient Native Americans show a single founding population that separated from its Asian relatives more than 20,000 years ago. Archaeological sites give minimum dates for when people were present. At Monte Verde, wooden posts, hearths, tools and food remains were preserved under a peat bog. At White Sands in New Mexico, human footprints run through layers of an old lake shore. Seeds in those layers were radiocarbon dated to between 23,000 and 21,000 years ago, and a later study reached similar ages from pollen and from quartz grains, using two other methods.

For most of the twentieth century, the accepted view was "Clovis first": that the earliest Americans were big-game hunters who walked through a gap between the ice sheets about 13,000 years ago. Monte Verde and other sites are older than that, and the gap between the ice sheets probably opened too late, so many researchers now favour a route down the Pacific coast. White Sands pushes the date much further back, to the coldest part of the ice age. Critics questioned the first dates because water plants can take up old carbon and look older than they are. The second study answered that objection for many researchers, but not all, and few other sites of that age have been found.

The peopling of the Americas completed the spread of our species across the habitable continents. It also began a separation: for more than 15,000 years, people in the Americas and people in Africa, Asia and Europe built farms, cities and states with no knowledge of each other. Chapter 7 tells what happened when the two halves met again.
